title: Quiet Crusts, Tested Hearts, and a Friend for Adversity
summary: The chapter prefers a dry crust in peace to a feast full of strife, and it moves through the LORD's testing of hearts, mockery of the poor, the workings of bribery, the damage of quarrels, and the grief of a foolish son. Its best known lines praise the friend who loves at all times and the brother born for adversity, and it ends with the observation that even a fool seems wise when he keeps quiet.
story: The second half of the Solomonic collection, which began in chapter 16, continues here with a mix of forms. The LORD's rule over human plans, so prominent in chapter 16, is now applied to relationships: households, friendships, courts, and neighbors. Chapter 17 is especially concerned with conflict, how it starts, how it spreads, and how it can be stopped. The foolish son of 10:1 returns in verses 21 and 25, a reminder that the collection is still a father's teaching to a son who will soon have a household of his own.
historical:
Verses 8, 15, 23, and 26 concern the courts. In ancient Israel justice was administered by elders at the city gate and, for larger matters, by royal officials and priests. The law strictly forbade bribes because a gift blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). Yet bribery was a constant problem, and the prophets repeatedly accused judges and rulers of taking them (Isaiah 1:23; Micah 3:11). Samuel's sons are remembered for exactly this failure (1 Samuel 8:3). Verse 15, which calls acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous detestable to the LORD, echoes the law's command to judges in Deuteronomy 25:1.

Verse 18 returns to suretyship. Striking hands was the gesture that sealed a pledge, much as a handshake seals an agreement today. A man who struck hands for his neighbor became legally responsible for his neighbor's debt.
cultural:
Verse 1 contrasts a dry morsel with a house full of feasting. The Hebrew for feasting is literally sacrifices, because the meat eaten at festive meals often came from fellowship offerings, where part of the animal was burned on the altar and the rest was eaten by the worshiper's household. A house full of sacrifices was a house of plenty and religious celebration. The saying prefers stale bread in quiet to that abundance soured by quarrels.

Verse 12 draws on a danger every shepherd knew. The Syrian brown bear lived in the hills of ancient Israel, and a mother bear robbed of her cubs was proverbial for fury (2 Samuel 17:8; Hosea 13:8). The saying is humorous and serious at once: better to meet her than a fool in the middle of his folly. Verse 3 draws on metalworking. Silver and gold were refined in a crucible or furnace that burned off the impurities, and the image of God refining his people recurs in the prophets (Isaiah 48:10; Malachi 3:3).
literary: The chapter is framed by sayings about quiet: a dry morsel in quietness (verse 1) and the fool who keeps silent (verse 28). Several groups stand out. Verses 9, 14, and 19 form a thread on quarrels, with the vivid image of a quarrel as water let loose, easy to release and impossible to call back (verse 14). Verses 21 and 25 both lament the fool's grief to his parents. The bribe appears twice, first described (verse 8) and then condemned (verse 23), and the pairing is instructive. Verse 3 sets the human refining of metals beside the LORD's testing of hearts, using a comparison without any verb. Verse 16 asks a mocking question about a fool paying tuition for wisdom he has no heart to learn, and verse 7 argues from lesser to greater with a how-much-worse.

outline.t: Quiet over feasting, the LORD who tests hearts, and the crown of the aged
Fitting speech, bribes, covering offenses, and returning evil for good
The fool's parents, a joyful heart, and the wisdom of silence

doctrines.note: The LORD tests hearts as fire tests silver and gold (verse 3). His holiness is not only his separation from sin but his searching presence, which refines the people he loves.

Perverting justice is detestable to the LORD (verse 15), and the one who gloats over calamity will not go unpunished (verse 5). God's judgment defends the innocent and the poor against corrupt courts and cruel neighbors.

Grandchildren are the crown of the aged and fathers the glory of sons (verse 6), but a foolish son grieves both parents (verses 21, 25). Friendship too is a kind of family: a brother is born for adversity (verse 17).

words.note: Shochad, bribe, a gift given to influence a judge or official. Verse 8 says it works like a charm (literally a stone of favor) for the giver, while verse 23 says the wicked man takes one to twist justice. The law forbade bribes because they blind the seeing, and the book's two sayings together show both why people give them and why God condemns them.

Mitsref, crucible, the clay vessel in which silver was heated so the dross could be skimmed off. The first line of verse 3 reappears in 27:21, where the test is a man's praise. The image of a crucible expresses a purpose in testing: the aim is not to destroy the metal but to purify it.

Re'a, neighbor, friend, companion. It is the word in the command to love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18). In verse 17 it names the friend who loves at all times. In verse 18 the same word names the neighbor for whom a foolish man pledges security, a reminder that loving a neighbor is not the same as putting one's household at risk for him.

christ: Verse 17's friend who loves at all times and brother born for adversity finds its fullest expression in Jesus, who called his disciples friends and said that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13-15), and who is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The link is thematic, not a prediction. Verse 15's condemnation of acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous raises a question the gospel answers directly. Paul says God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), which would be exactly the injustice verse 15 condemns, except that God does it through the cross, where the righteous one bore the penalty so that God could be both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26). The New Testament takes verse 15's standard seriously; that is why the cross was necessary.

hard.q: Verse 8 says a bribe works like a charm. Is the Bible endorsing bribery?
hard.a:
No. This is one of the clearest examples of a proverb that observes rather than commends. Verse 8 describes how bribes look from the giver's side: they open doors and smooth the way. Anyone in the ancient world, or ours, knew that to be true. But the same chapter condemns the wicked man who takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice (verse 23), and the law forbids bribes outright (Exodus 23:8). Reading verse 8 as advice would pull it out of its setting in the book.

Some interpreters see verse 8 as ironic, voicing the briber's own view of his gift, which the reader is meant to see through. Others think it is simply realistic, teaching the young to understand how power works so that they will not be naive. A few scholars distinguish between a bribe that perverts justice and a gift given to gain a hearing (compare 18:16 and 21:14), noting that Proverbs describes both without always passing judgment. On any reading, the book's overall verdict is clear: justice that can be bought is detestable to the LORD.

questions: Verse 9 says covering an offense promotes love, while repeating it separates friends. When is it right to let something go, and when must it be addressed?
Verse 17 describes a friend who loves at all times. Who has been that friend to you, and to whom could you be that friend now?
Verse 14 compares starting a quarrel to releasing a flood. What habits help you stop a dispute before it breaks out?
